verses.text: The sons of the prophets said to Elisha, “See now, the place where we live and meet with you is too small for us.
Please let us go to the Jordan, and each man take a beam from there, and let us make us a place there, where we may live.” He answered, “Go!”
One said, “Please be pleased to go with your servants.” He answered, “I will go.”
So he went with them. When they came to the Jordan, they cut down wood.
But as one was cutting down a tree, the ax head fell into the water. Then he cried, and said, “Alas, my master! For it was borrowed.”
The man of God asked, “Where did it fall?” He showed him the place. He cut down a stick, threw it in there, and made the iron float.
He said, “Take it.” So he put out his hand and took it.
Now the king of Syria was at war against Israel; and he took counsel with his servants, saying, “My camp will be in such and such a place.”
The man of God sent to the king of Israel, saying, “Beware that you not pass this place; for the Syrians are coming down there.”
The king of Israel sent to the place which the man of God told him and warned him of; and he saved himself there, not once or twice.
The king of Syria’s heart was very troubled about this. He called his servants, and said to them, “Won’t you show me which of us is for the king of Israel?”
One of his servants said, “No, my lord, O king; but Elisha, the prophet who is in Israel, tells the king of Israel the words that you speak in your bedroom.”
He said, “Go and see where he is, that I may send and get him.” He was told, “Behold, he is in Dothan.”
Therefore he sent horses, chariots, and a great army there. They came by night, and surrounded the city.
When the servant of the man of God had risen early, and gone out, behold, an army with horses and chariots was around the city. His servant said to him, “Alas, my master! What shall we do?”
He answered, “Don’t be afraid; for those who are with us are more than those who are with them.”

Elisha prayed, and said, “Yahweh, please open his eyes, that he may see.” Yahweh opened the young man’s eyes; and he saw: and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha.
When they came down to him, Elisha prayed to Yahweh, and said, “Please strike this people with blindness.” He struck them with blindness according to Elishah’s word.
Elisha said to them, “This is not the way, neither is this the city. Follow me, and I will bring you to the man whom you seek.” He led them to Samaria.
When they had come into Samaria, Elisha said, “Yahweh, open these men’s eyes, that they may see.” Yahweh opened their eyes, and they saw; and behold, they were in the middle of Samaria.
The king of Israel said to Elisha, when he saw them, “My father, shall I strike them? Shall I strike them?”

He answered, “You shall not strike them. Would you strike those whom you have taken captive with your sword and with your bow? Set bread and water before them, that they may eat and drink, and go to their master.”
He prepared great feast for them. When they had eaten and drunk, he sent them away, and they went to their master. So the bands of Syria stopped raiding the land of Israel.
After this, Benhadad king of Syria gathered all his army, and went up and besieged Samaria.
There was a great famine in Samaria. Behold, they besieged it, until a donkey’s head was sold for eighty pieces of silver, and the fourth part of a kab  of dove’s dung for five pieces of silver.
As the king of Israel was passing by on the wall, a woman cried to him, saying, “Help, my lord, O king!”
He said, “If Yahweh doesn’t help you, where could I get help for you? From of the threshing floor, or from the wine press?”
The king said to her, “What is your problem?” She answered, “This woman said to me, ‘Give your son, that we may eat him today, and we will eat my son tomorrow.’
So we boiled my son, and ate him: and I said to her on the next day, ‘Give your son, that we may eat him;’ and she has hidden her son.”
When the king heard the words of the woman, he tore his clothes. Now he was passing by on the wall, and the people looked, and behold, he had sackcloth underneath on his body.
Then he said, “God do so to me, and more also, if the head of Elisha the son of Shaphat stays on him today.”

But Elisha was sitting in his house, and the elders were sitting with him. Then the king sent a man from before him; but before the messenger came to him, he said to the elders, “Do you see how this son of a murderer has sent to take away my head? Behold, when the messenger comes, shut the door, and hold the door shut against him. Isn’t the sound of his master’s feet behind him?”
While he was still talking with them, behold, the messenger came down to him. Then he said, “Behold, this evil is from Yahweh. Why should I wait for Yahweh any longer?”

footnotes.content: Growing pains, even in God's household—the prophets are thriving so much their lodging bursts at the seams. I see in this the Father's delight when His people multiply. Prosperity brings its own small tests; how we handle them says much.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Notice they ask permission, ask for Elisha's company. Humble submission marks a healthy school. The Jordan, where Israel crossed into the land—now these servants go there to build anew. There's a rhythm to it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One brave soul asks Elisha to come along himself. His 'I will go' is so simple—he doesn't defer or claim to be too weary. That's the servant heart I have always loved: ready to be where the need is.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Work and wood, the honest, ordinary stuff of building. Elisha goes with them to the Jordan to saw and sweat alongside. It tells you everything about a true leader.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The ax head falls into the water—and it was borrowed. There's the pinch: not his own tool, so the loss feels like betrayal, like failure before his master. Elisha hears the cry of despair and answers it. That's the God I know: He leans toward the cry of the small.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A stick thrown into water, and iron floats. I know better than to puzzle over the mechanics—what matters is that Elisha's prayer reshapes the world. When the impossible becomes ordinary, we're in the hands of One who made both water and metal.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Take it.' One word, and recovery. The servant reaches out and retrieves what was lost. I see Christ's hand reaching toward us—Come, take, believe. The borrowed ax is returned; the shame lifts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The scene shifts now to war rooms and strategy. Ben-Hadad of Syria thinks his counsel hidden, his camps secret. But there is One who hears all words in all bedrooms. The mighty forget they are not alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elisha sends warning to Israel's king—beware, the enemy camps there. How does he know? He doesn't run; he doesn't scheme. He prays and speaks, and the Lord shields His own. That's the confidence of a man who knows his place in God's hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Not once or twice—the pattern repeats. Israel's king learns to trust the word and is saved again and again. Faithfulness confirmed in repetition builds deep roots. How many times must the Lord prove faithful before we believe He will again?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ben-Hadad's heart is troubled—something keeps spoiling his plans. He suspects a traitor in his midst, yet none of his servants owns the truth. The guilty always wonder who saw them. Fear, not faith, drives his next move.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One servant speaks truth: Elisha hears the words spoken in private chambers. How frightening to be known so completely, yet how liberating if we surrender to the One who sees all. There's no hiding place but His shadow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Dothan—a place I've walked in thought many times. Here Abraham once pitched his tent; now Elisha sits, and the king of Syria sends his whole army to seize one old prophet. It's a measure of how much Elisha's words terrify the powerful.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Horses, chariots, a great army—all night they march to corner one man. The weight of such effort tells you: the throne fears God's voice more than God's absence. By night they come because they hope darkness hides their shame.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The servant wakes to horses and chariots ringing the city—a child's terror at a sight too great to hold. 'What shall we do?' The question that freezes the heart. In every age, the young see the trap before seeing the Deliverer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Don't be afraid; for those who are with us are more than those who are with them.' Elisha's calm is not bravado—it's the settled conviction of a man who has looked into the unseen realm and seen the Lord's abundance there. Fear and faith cannot share the same breath.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elisha prays that eyes be opened, and the mountain is full of horses and chariots of fire—the actual substance of the kingdom's protection, hidden from ordinary sight. This is not metaphor; it is daily reality veiled from our closed eyes. How many fiery guardians surround us unperceived?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elisha prays again—this time for the enemy to be struck blind. God answers according to His servant's word. A power like this is terrifying; that it serves mercy and not vengeance shows the character of the one who wields it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Blinded, they are lost—and Elisha becomes their guide. 'Follow me,' he says, and leads them not to slaughter but deeper into the trap that will become their mercy. The sightless follow the prophet who sees. There's a parable for all of us here.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Once more, Elisha prays—'Open these men's eyes.' Sight returns, and they find themselves in Samaria, surrounded and helpless. The blindness lifts too late to run. They are in the hand of Israel's king with no escape.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Israel's king sees the captured Syrians and asks Elisha the warrior's question: 'Shall I strike them? Shall I strike them?' The natural heart cries for blood, for settlement, for closure through force. Even victory tempts us to sin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'You shall not strike them.' Elisha commands mercy. Instead: bread and water, a feast, the dignity of men sent home alive. This is the hardest victory—to defeat an enemy and then feed him. But it is the victory that changes hearts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A great feast prepared, and the bands of Syria stopped raiding. Mercy accomplished what swords could not. The enemy fills his belly, meets the kindness of his captors, and the war ends—not by victory, but by transformation. This is Christ's way: overcome evil with good.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But Ben-Hadad will not be taught by mercy. He gathers his whole army again and lays siege to Samaria. There are hearts so fixed on pride that kindness only looks like weakness. The lesson is lost.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Great famine in the besieged city—donkey's head for eighty pieces of silver, dove's dung for food. The siege strip bare all dignity and plenty. Starvation speaks in prices that make you weep. This is what war brings when it comes home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A woman's voice pierces the king's ear as he walks the wall. 'Help, my lord, O king!' The desperate cry that finds the power-holder. In hunger and despair, she sees only the king as deliverer. But even he is bound by the siege.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He asks where help could come from—threshing floor or wine press? Empty metaphors for empty larders. The king admits his helplessness. In extremity, rulers too must confess they are small. Only then might we turn to the One who is not.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'What is your problem?' he asks, and she answers with horror: a pact with another mother to eat one another's sons. Famine has driven them to cannibalism—the outer wall of civilization crumbles when hunger is master. Her confession is the breaking of every taboo, every hope.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'We boiled my son and ate him.' The words sit in silence, unspeakable and irreversible. She begged the other mother to keep her part of the bargain, but the woman hid her son. Even in extremity, we betray—hunger makes monsters of us all.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king tears his clothes, reveals sackcloth already worn beneath. He has been mourning all along, yet it changes nothing. Outward sorrow without repentance is just theater. The city starves while the king grieves his powerlessness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In his rage, the king swears Elisha's head will fall. He calls him 'son of a murderer'—perhaps Elisha's father was Shaphat, or perhaps the king simply cannot bear that the prophet does not share his panic. We blame the messenger when we cannot blame God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elisha sits calm with the elders, unafraid of the coming messenger. He knows the king has sent a man to kill him—how does he know? He has already spoken what will come. 'Shut the door. Do you hear the master's feet behind him?' Faith speaks plainly when it sees God's nearness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king arrives himself, crying 'This evil is from Yahweh. Why wait for Him any longer?' In despair's last breath, he confesses—God, not Syria, has brought this. Readers today hear an echo: in our hungriest hour, do we blame God or turn to Him? The question outlasts the siege.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
